events.title: HTTP/1.1 standardized
events.summary: RFC 2068 defined HTTP/1.1 in January 1997 — adding persistent connections, chunked transfer, and better caching than HTTP/1.0.
events.about: HTTP/1.1 is how browsers and APIs talk to servers — GET/POST requests, status codes, headers. Persistent connections cut latency; virtual hosts let one IP serve many domains. Every REST API, CDN, and `fetch()` call still rides on HTTP semantics defined here and refined in later RFCs.

narrative.whyChosen: HTTP/1.1 fixed the performance and proxy problems that limited HTTP/1.0 at web scale.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the wire protocol underpinning the web, APIs, and eventually HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.
narrative.problemSolved: HTTP/1.0 opened a new TCP connection per request and handled caching inconsistently.

events.title: PostgreSQL 6.0 released
events.summary: PostgreSQL 6.0 shipped on January 29, 1997 — adopting the PostgreSQL name and SQL support atop Berkeley's POSTGRES research codebase.
events.about: PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database with strong SQL, JSON, and extension support — used for SaaS backends, geospatial (PostGIS), and analytics. Teams pick it for ACID guarantees, complex queries, and no vendor lock-in. Example: a Rails or Django app with migrations, foreign keys, and full-text search on one Postgres instance.

narrative.whyChosen: PostgreSQL carried Berkeley POSTGRES into production as a mainstream open-source RDBMS.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the default 'serious' open-source SQL database for startups and enterprises alike.
narrative.problemSolved: Postgres95 needed a durable name and version line as SQL features matured beyond research prototypes.
